question.problem: If ${f}^{′}(x)=-|x+2|,$ which of the following could be the graph of a continuous function $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/0bfc917724b8339ef52888f287f2bc1c69fca41e9207f42ff3d83a633fe3cc0a.png)

Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point: 

$\,$ $x=-2$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $-2$ | $(-2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{no extr.}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=-2,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/d032eca4d1a29d5a7809dfd5c43cce52b8a0b66f1c8bdc9b9747cf704da524f5.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-2)$ and is decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left of $x=-2$ and goes down to the right of $x=-2.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=-2$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x=-2$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ So, $x=-2$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

So, we can draw as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/ba965ae91587d92beee6b5acb9af809167bb1de01fe1c2cdb8b0637244356e7f.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/fbe2e07c3c82e1140e2e9d687020ece8dad208251dfeec2bddbd27bc5c44841d.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
